titulo: Unplugging your phone charger saves pennies, not dollars
receta: error cotidiano con regla para guardar + pregunta de dos bandos (yes or no)
destinatario: se lo manda quien paga la cuenta de luz a su amigo o pareja que desenchufa cada cargador pero deja la tele y la consola en standby
regla_guardable: One idle charger: under a dollar a year. All standby power in a house: 5 to 10 percent of its electricity. Put the TV setup on one power strip and switch it off.

interaccion.guardar: One typical idle charger: about $0.76 a year at most (0.5 W). Standby power in a home: an estimated 5-10% of its electricity. TV setup on one power strip, switch it off.
interaccion.comentar: Do you unplug your chargers? Yes or no?

fuentes: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Standby Power (standby.lbl.gov): standby power is 5-10% of residential electricity use; most products draw less than 0.5 watts; TVs, microwave ovens and air conditioners are examples of products that draw standby power
U.S. EIA: average U.S. residential electricity price 17.30 cents per kWh in 2025 (preliminary)
Own arithmetic: 0.5 W x 8,760 h = 4.38 kWh x $0.173 = about $0.76 a year

frases.texto: You unplug your phone charger every morning to save money.
frases.estilo: Dry, direct, with a half smile.

frases.texto: Here's the math. Most products that draw standby power use less than half a watt, says Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.
Even if a charger drew half a watt all year, that's about four kilowatt-hours. At the average U.S. rate, roughly seventy-six cents.
So one charger is pennies. But the whole house adds up: Berkeley Lab estimates standby power is five to ten percent of home electricity.
So skip the single charger. Put the TV setup on one power strip, and switch it off, like the Energy Department suggests.
Heads up: a cable DVR or console may need power to record or update, and your savings depend on your rate.
